Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Mauricio Funes was inaugurated Monday as El Salvador's president, promising to work for the nation's poor and disadvantaged. El Salvador's new president, Mauricio Funes, takes power Monday after his inauguration in San Salvador. Funes, elected March 15, is a member of a political party that waged guerrilla war against the government 17 years ago. He is El Salvador's first leftist president. "The Salvadoran public asked for a change, and that change begins now," Funes said in an inauguration speech before an audience that included Latin American leaders and U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. Funes, a member of the FMLN party, won a narrow victory over the ARENA party's Rodrigo Avila. Funes' victory ended a 20-year hold on the presidency by the right-leaning ARENA. With Funes' win, El Salvador joined other Latin American countries that have elected leftist leaders in recent years -- Venezuela, Bolivia, Nicaragua, Argentina, Honduras, Guatemala, Ecuador and Brazil. The FMLN, which is the Spanish acronym for the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front, was formed in 1980 as an umbrella group for five leftist guerilla organizations fighting a U.S.-backed military dictatorship. The guerrillas and the government signed a peace pact in 1992, and the FMLN became a legitimate political party. By some estimates, 75,000 Salvadorans died during the war. The new president will find "a country that still retains a lot of bitterness, a lot of division," Peter Hakim, president of the Washington-based Inter-American Dialogue policy institute, said before the election. "This country is completely divided," ARENA party official Adolfo Torres said on CNN affiliate TCS TV on election night. Funes acknowledged that division Monday, promising to "create a country without hate and without resentment." He also seemed to acknowledge the difficulties ahead, saying, "We don't have the right to make mistakes." Despite a dire economy, Funes promised an ambitious social program that would include construction of 11,000 homes, scholarships for children ages 6 to 18 and improvement in delivery of water, electricity and sanitary services to 32 poor municipalities. He may be hard-pressed to follow through, some analysts said. "Once Funes assumes office on 1 June, his government will face major challenges to boost the economy, cut government expenditures to trim the fiscal deficit and maintain support to the poor, who are being hit hardest by the economic downturn," analyst Heather Berkman wrote in a report last week for the Eurasia Group consulting firm. "Cutting expenditures and reducing the deficit will be the most important challenges," Berkman wrote, adding that to "do this, the Funes administration plans to cut government spending and eliminate redundant presidential commissions; retarget propane subsidies (and perhaps eventually eliminate them); and propose a number of new taxes on alcoholic beverages, tobacco and new vehicles." Funes campaigned on a platform of fiscal reform that aims to increase the government's tax take incrementally, Berkman said. Funes did not offer any details Monday, speaking instead in general terms of the El Salvador he would like to see under his five-year administration. He will not, Funes said, "govern for a few or be complacent to corruption." Funes, a former freelance journalist for CNN en Español, noted in particular that his administration will fight organized crime and narcotraffickers. "In this government," he said, "those who have merit will be compensated and those who are guilty will be punished."

(CNN) — Mauricio Funes was sworn in as president of El Salvador on Monday in San Salvador, pledging to serve the country’s impoverished and disadvantaged citizens.

Funes, who won the March 15 election, became El Salvador’s first left-wing president. He belongs to a party that fought a guerrilla war against the government 17 years earlier.

“The Salvadoran public asked for a change, and that change begins now,” Funes told an inauguration audience that included leaders from across Latin America and U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.

Representing the FMLN, Funes narrowly defeated Rodrigo Avila of the ARENA party. His election brought an end to the right-leaning ARENA’s 20-year control of the presidency. It also placed El Salvador among a group of Latin American nations that had elected leftist leaders in recent years, including Venezuela, Bolivia, Nicaragua, Argentina, Honduras, Guatemala, Ecuador and Brazil.

The initials FMLN stand in Spanish for the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. The organization was established in 1980 as a coalition of five leftist guerrilla groups fighting a U.S.-supported military dictatorship. After the rebels and the government reached a peace agreement in 1992, the FMLN became a legally recognized political party. Some estimates put the number of Salvadorans killed during the conflict at 75,000.

Before the election, Peter Hakim, president of the Washington-based Inter-American Dialogue policy institute, said the incoming president would inherit “a country that still retains a lot of bitterness, a lot of division.”

On election night, ARENA official Adolfo Torres similarly told CNN affiliate TCS TV, “This country is completely divided.”

Funes addressed those tensions during his inauguration, vowing to “create a country without hate and without resentment.” He also recognized the scale of the challenges facing his administration, declaring, “We don’t have the right to make mistakes.”

Although El Salvador’s economy was in severe difficulty, Funes outlined an extensive social agenda. His proposals included building 11,000 homes, providing scholarships for children between the ages of 6 and 18, and improving access to water, electricity and sanitation in 32 poor municipalities.

Some analysts warned that fulfilling those commitments could prove difficult. Heather Berkman, an analyst with the Eurasia Group consulting firm, wrote in a report the previous week that after taking office on June 1, Funes would confront significant obstacles. She said his government would need to stimulate economic growth, reduce public spending to narrow the fiscal deficit, and continue assisting poor Salvadorans, who were suffering most from the economic downturn.

According to Berkman, the administration’s foremost tasks would be lowering expenditures and shrinking the deficit. She said Funes planned to pursue those goals by cutting government spending, abolishing unnecessary presidential commissions, redirecting propane subsidies—and possibly eliminating them eventually—and proposing new taxes on alcohol, tobacco and new vehicles.

Berkman also said Funes had run on a fiscal-reform platform designed to increase government tax revenue gradually.

In his Monday address, however, Funes did not provide specifics. Instead, he spoke broadly about the kind of El Salvador he hoped to build during his five-year term. He promised that he would not “govern for a few or be complacent to corruption.”

Funes, who previously worked as a freelance journalist for CNN en Español, also emphasized that his government would combat organized crime and drug traffickers.

“In this government,” he said, “those who have merit will be compensated and those who are guilty will be punished.”

# Funes inaugurated as El Salvador’s first leftist president

**SAN SALVADOR, El Salvador (CNN)** — Mauricio Funes was sworn in Monday as El Salvador’s first leftist president, ending two decades of conservative rule and marking a historic political transition in a country once divided by civil war.

Funes, a former television journalist, took office before regional leaders and international dignitaries after winning the March 2009 presidential election as the candidate of the Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front, or FMLN.

In his inaugural address, Funes promised to govern as a moderate and focus on El Salvador’s deep social and economic problems. His campaign emphasized job creation, expanded health care and education, affordable housing and assistance for poor families. He also pledged to fight corruption, tax evasion and the violent crime that has made El Salvador one of the most dangerous countries in the region.

Funes sought during the campaign to reassure business leaders and Washington that his administration would not pursue sweeping nationalizations or abandon close ties with the United States. He frequently cited former Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva as a model, presenting himself as a pragmatic leftist who would combine social spending with fiscal responsibility.

His inauguration represented a dramatic milestone for the FMLN, which began as a coalition of Marxist guerrilla organizations during El Salvador’s 1980-1992 civil war. The conflict between the military-backed government and leftist rebels killed an estimated 75,000 people and displaced hundreds of thousands more.

After peace accords were signed in 1992, the FMLN disarmed and became a political party. It gradually emerged as the principal opposition to the conservative Nationalist Republican Alliance, known as ARENA, which had controlled the presidency since 1989.

Funes was not a guerrilla commander and joined the FMLN only shortly before becoming its presidential candidate, helping the party broaden its appeal beyond its traditional base. His victory also reflected voter frustration over inequality, crime and the cost of living.

The new president takes office amid severe economic pressures. El Salvador’s economy was being hit by the global financial crisis and the recession in the United States, its largest trading partner. Exports and investment had weakened, while remittances sent home by Salvadorans living abroad — a crucial source of income for many families — were declining.

Poverty and underemployment remained widespread, and the government faced limited revenue, rising debt and demands for greater social spending. El Salvador’s use of the U.S. dollar, adopted in 2001, also left the administration with little control over monetary policy.

Funes acknowledged that fulfilling his campaign promises would be difficult but said the change in government offered the country a chance to move beyond ideological divisions.

His central challenge will be turning the symbolism of the FMLN’s peaceful rise to power into economic gains for Salvadorans while maintaining investor confidence and political stability.

## Mauricio Funes takes office in El Salvador — June 1, 2009

Mauricio Funes was sworn in as president of El Salvador on June 1, 2009, becoming the first leader from the left-wing Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front, or FMLN, to govern the country. A former television journalist who had not been a guerrilla commander, Funes defeated ARENA candidate Rodrigo Ávila in the March election with about 51.3 percent of the vote.

### Political significance

Funes’s victory ended 20 consecutive years of rule by the conservative Nationalist Republican Alliance, ARENA, which had held the presidency since 1989. It also carried powerful historical symbolism: the FMLN had fought the Salvadoran government as a guerrilla coalition during the 1980–1992 civil war before disarming and becoming a political party under the 1992 peace accords.

The inauguration therefore represented:

- **The first transfer of presidential power from the right to the left in modern Salvadoran history.**
- **A major test of the institutions created by the peace settlement**, showing that a former armed insurgency could reach power through elections.
- **A repudiation of ARENA’s long incumbency**, amid public dissatisfaction over inequality, unemployment, crime, corruption allegations, and the effects of the global economic crisis.
- **A shift toward Latin America’s broader leftward trend**, although Funes presented himself as a moderate social democrat rather than a radical populist. He often pointed to Brazil’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva as a model.

The narrow result also required caution. ARENA remained a major political force, while business groups and the United States watched closely for signs of how far an FMLN administration would move away from existing economic and foreign policies.

### Main themes of the inauguration speech

Funes used his inaugural address to emphasize reconciliation and pragmatic reform rather than ideological retaliation. He declared that his government would serve all Salvadorans and said the election should close an era of exclusion, confrontation, and one-party dominance.

His principal messages included:

- **National unity and reconciliation:** Funes promised not to govern for the FMLN alone and rejected revenge against political opponents. He called for cooperation among parties, business, labor, and civil society.
- **Priority for the poor:** He pledged to make marginalized Salvadorans the central concern of government through expanded health, education, housing, pensions, and employment programs.
- **Economic recovery:** Taking office during the global recession, he proposed measures to stimulate production, support agriculture and small businesses, build infrastructure, and protect families affected by unemployment and declining remittances.
- **Honest and austere government:** Funes promised transparency, a campaign against corruption, and responsible use of public funds. He portrayed ethical government as essential to restoring trust in the state.
- **Public security:** He acknowledged violent crime and gang activity as urgent national problems and advocated a strategy combining effective policing with prevention and social opportunities for young people.
- **Moderation and institutional continuity:** He reassured investors and foreign partners that change would occur within democratic and constitutional rules, not through abrupt revolutionary transformation.
- **A more independent foreign policy:** His government moved immediately to restore diplomatic relations with Cuba, which El Salvador had severed in 1961, while also affirming the importance of maintaining strong relations with the United States.

Overall, Funes framed his inauguration as the beginning of a peaceful democratic transformation: a government rooted in the left’s historic struggle but committed to pluralism, social inclusion, and gradual reform.

**Funes takes office in El Salvador, pledging aid for poor and national reconciliation**

**SAN SALVADOR, June 1, 2009** — Mauricio Funes was sworn in Monday as president of El Salvador, becoming the first leftist leader elected since the country’s civil war and ending two decades of conservative rule with promises to fight poverty, corruption and organized crime.

Funes, a former television journalist who ran for the Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front, or FMLN, called for national unity in a country still divided by the legacy of the 1980-1992 conflict. He said his government would give priority to poor families while pursuing responsible economic and fiscal policies.

“The time has come for national unity,” Funes told lawmakers, foreign dignitaries and political leaders at the inauguration ceremony in San Salvador. He said his victory should not be understood as one part of the country defeating another, but as an opportunity to overcome old political and social divisions.

The FMLN, once a coalition of guerrilla organizations, became a political party under the 1992 peace accords that ended a 12-year civil war in which about 75,000 people were killed. Funes’s inauguration marked the first peaceful transfer of power to the left in El Salvador’s modern history.

He succeeded Antonio Saca of the conservative Nationalist Republican Alliance, or ARENA, which had governed since 1989. Funes defeated ARENA candidate Rodrigo Ávila in the March election with just over 51 percent of the vote.

Funes promised a government focused on those hardest hit by unemployment, high food prices and the global economic downturn. El Salvador’s economy was under pressure from declining exports, investment and remittances sent by Salvadorans living abroad, particularly in the United States.

Among his priorities, Funes outlined emergency social measures intended to create jobs, support low-income households and improve access to education and health care. His administration planned assistance including school meals, uniforms and supplies for children in public schools, expanded health services, housing construction and modest pensions for elderly people in the poorest communities.

He said public policy would be guided by a “preferential option” for the poor, while insisting that social spending must be accompanied by better management of government finances.

The new president also pledged fiscal reform, arguing that the state needed more reliable revenue to finance essential services and development. Rather than placing the burden on ordinary wage earners and consumers, Funes said the government would seek to curb tax evasion, improve collection and make the tax system fairer.

Any broad fiscal overhaul was expected to require negotiation with opposition parties and the private sector. The FMLN did not control enough seats in the Legislative Assembly to act alone, making compromise central to Funes’s ability to carry out his agenda.

Funes also made the fight against corruption a prominent part of his inaugural address. He promised transparency in public spending, stricter oversight of state institutions and investigations into misuse of government resources.

“No one will be above the law,” he said, presenting honesty in government as essential to restoring public confidence.

Public security posed another immediate challenge. El Salvador had one of the highest homicide rates in the world, driven by street gangs, drug trafficking, extortion and increasingly sophisticated criminal networks. Funes promised to strengthen the police, improve intelligence and coordination among security agencies, and confront organized crime without abandoning crime-prevention and rehabilitation programs.

He said the government would distinguish between poverty and criminality, rejecting policies that treated marginalized young people as automatic suspects. At the same time, he vowed firm action against gangs, traffickers and criminal organizations that had penetrated communities and institutions.

Funes sought during the campaign to portray himself as a moderate rather than an ideological radical. In his inaugural speech, he indicated that El Salvador would maintain close relations with the United States, home to more than two million Salvadorans and the source of billions of dollars in annual remittances.

He also emphasized stronger relations with Latin American countries and announced the restoration of diplomatic ties with Cuba, severed after the Cuban Revolution 50 years earlier. The move left El Salvador as the last Central American country to renew formal relations with Havana.

Foreign leaders and senior officials attended the ceremony, including U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and several Latin American presidents. Their presence underscored the regional importance of the transition and the expectation that Funes could position El Salvador’s government between the region’s more radical leftist administrations and its conservative allies.

Funes took office alongside Vice President Salvador Sánchez Cerén, a former guerrilla commander and senior FMLN figure. Their partnership reflected the coalition behind the new government: Funes represented a more independent and centrist public image, while Sánchez Cerén embodied the party’s historic leadership.

The president acknowledged that expectations were high but warned that El Salvador’s problems could not be solved immediately. He inherited strained public finances, widespread poverty, weak economic growth and severe insecurity.

His central message was that political change must translate into practical improvements for citizens who had long felt excluded.

Funes said his administration would seek dialogue with business leaders, labor unions, churches, civil society groups and opposition parties to develop national agreements on economic recovery, security and fiscal policy.

After years in which politics was shaped by memories of war and ideological confrontation, Funes presented his inauguration as the beginning of a new stage.

“My government will be a government of national unity,” he said, pledging to govern not only for the voters who supported the FMLN but for all Salvadorans.

Funes, a 49-year-old former television journalist, won the March 2009 election as the candidate of the Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front, or FMLN. His victory marked the first time the left had captured the presidency in El Salvador.

“The time has come for the excluded,” Funes said in his inaugural address. “The opportunity has come for those who never had an opportunity.”

Funes sought to reassure business leaders and foreign governments that his administration would not follow the more confrontational path of some leftist governments in Latin America. He presented himself as a moderate reformer and cited Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva as a political model.

“This will be a government of national unity,” Funes said, promising to govern not only for the FMLN but for all Salvadorans.

His inauguration represented a dramatic change for a country still shaped by a 12-year civil war that killed about 75,000 people and displaced hundreds of thousands more. From 1980 to 1992, the U.S.-backed Salvadoran government fought the FMLN, then a coalition of five guerrilla organizations. The conflict was marked by massacres, death-squad killings and widespread human rights abuses.

The 1992 peace accords ended the fighting, reduced the military’s political role and transformed the FMLN into a legal political party. The former rebels gradually gained strength in Congress and municipal governments but repeatedly lost presidential elections to the right-wing Nationalist Republican Alliance, known as ARENA.

Political analysts described Funes’ victory as evidence that El Salvador’s democratic system had matured since the peace accords. Cynthia Arnson, a Latin America specialist at the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars, called the peaceful transfer of power “an extraordinary accomplishment” for a country whose political divisions had once been settled by armed conflict.

Analysts also said Funes’ background distinguished him from the FMLN’s former guerrilla commanders. As a prominent interviewer and television presenter, he built a reputation for questioning government officials and investigating corruption, but he did not fight in the civil war.

Michael Shifter of the Inter-American Dialogue described the election as a “historic turning point,” while cautioning that Funes would have to balance the expectations of the FMLN’s traditional base with the concerns of investors, the middle class and Washington.

Funes entered office amid a global recession, falling exports and remittances, persistent poverty and some of the highest violent-crime rates in the Western Hemisphere. His economic program called for increased social spending while maintaining the U.S. dollar as El Salvador’s official currency.

Among his principal proposals was a large-scale housing program intended to build about 25,000 homes and generate construction jobs. He also promised scholarships and expanded educational assistance for young people from low-income families.

Funes said his government would invest in roads, schools, hospitals and other public infrastructure, both to modernize the country and to stimulate employment during the downturn. Other plans included expanded health services, school meals and support for small businesses and agricultural producers.

Financing those programs could prove difficult. Funes said he would seek additional revenue by combating tax evasion, improving customs collection and requiring wealthier Salvadorans and large companies to meet their obligations. He stopped short of proposing an immediate, sweeping increase in tax rates.

At the same time, he promised austerity within the government. Funes said unnecessary official travel, luxury vehicles, advertising and other nonessential expenditures would be reduced so money could be redirected toward social programs.

“We are going to spend less on the government and more on the people,” he said.

His administration’s room to maneuver was expected to be limited by public debt, weak economic growth and the FMLN’s lack of an outright legislative majority. Funes would need support from smaller parties—or at times from ARENA—to pass budgets, tax measures and major reforms.

Relations with the United States were another early test. Washington backed the Salvadoran government during the civil war and remained the country’s largest trading partner and home to more than 2 million Salvadorans. Funes said he wanted close relations with the United States while also expanding ties across Latin America.

For supporters gathered in San Salvador, however, the inauguration carried meaning beyond policy. It completed the FMLN’s transformation from an armed insurgency into a governing party and demonstrated that power could change hands through elections.

Funes acknowledged that history while emphasizing reconciliation.

“The past cannot be changed,” he said. “But the future can be built differently.”
